sections.title: Policy and access to the centre
sections.text:
Our Marseille data is recent, so there is no city trend yet; the figures below cover only the 15 car parks we measure, for weekdays and weekends in August and September 2026.

Marseille has taken cars out of the Vieux-Port and the Canebière step by step. A Métropole leaflet announced that from July 2019 the Canebière would be closed to general traffic between the Vieux-Port and rue Paradis, with bollards for police, rescue and deliveries, and that buses would stop using the stretch [0]. Paid street parking has spread outward: in October 2019 it was extended to about 130 streets in five central districts, with 2,618 spaces and 134 new meters [1]. A parking-plan leaflet lists on-street rates of €1.50 for an hour and €6 for four in the yellow zone, €8 for four hours in the hypercentre, and resident subscriptions of €130 a year [6]. The low-emission zone started in September 2022 with Crit'Air 5 vehicles [3]. In February 2024 the Métropole's president announced that its planned extension to Crit'Air 3 would not be applied, with no new date [4]. A national attempt to repeal such zones was struck down in May 2026 [5]. Park-and-ride was opened at weekends on trial in 2019 [7].

sections.title: Parking developments
sections.text:
Few changes to the stock appear in our sources. The La Fourragère park-and-ride reopened in 2023 with 794 spaces, up from 492, and rooftop solar panels [8]. In Belsunce the 80-space Providence car park, closed since 2022 when its concession ended, was cleared in March 2024 to make way for a planted public square, with delivery forecast for 2026 [9]. On charging, ENGIE said it would have 250 street charge points across 25 communes by the end of 2024, and the release does not mention car parks [10]. The Métropole publishes the location and capacity of the gated car parks it owns as open data, though not live availability [11].

Demand from outside is strong. Local tourism officials said the 2024 Olympic sailing events boosted summer overnight stays, international ones by 38% [12], the port carried 4.1 million sea passengers in 2025, nearly two-thirds of them on cruise ships [13], and public transport use has grown from 509,000 trips a day in 2006 to over 900,000 in 2024 [14].

sections.title: Operators, location, price and use
sections.text:
Marseille's car parks are dear and, where we measure them, well used: the 15 average 57% on weekdays and 52% at weekends. Indigo's central garages charge about €3.60–4.40 an hour and mostly €31–38 a day, roughly 12% above their neighbours in our research set, and still fill: Charles de Gaulle (70%), République (72%), Jean Jaurès (69%) and Castellane (67%). Q-Park's Vieux-Port garage, a little cheaper at €3.00, is at 63%, and its two outer garages at Vallier and Blancarde, at €2.10 an hour and €14.60 a day, are the fullest we measure (77% and 75%). Effia's garages are the cheapest at €2.40, with day tickets of €15.50, but they are quieter: Monthyon 47%, Cours Julien 23%, and the small Corderie 2%.

Not every central car park is busy. Baret Saint-Ferréol (350 spaces) stands at 6% and Espercieux at 4%, while the Préfecture garage stands at 53%. Some empty at weekends: Monthyon drops from 47% to 17% and Cours Julien from 23% to 6%. We cannot yet say much about Q-Park's and Indigo's other car parks, where our research set has few capacities and no measurements.
